text: The document is intended to describe best practices for O-RAN Architecture and Solution for X-haul timing & synchronization. Beyond the solutions described in this document, other Architectures and Solutions may be adequate for X-haul timing & synchronization and can be considered in future versions of this document.
trace: 3 Scope

text: As far as possible it tries to make no assumptions, rather define overall Open X-haul synchronization solution and architecture model, to enable the operators to understand different synchronization options and deployment models and help them to come up with right network sync model that can support the different 5G services, the different radio architectures.
trace: 3 Scope

text: The section 6 concentrates on a general description of timing and synchronization technology, different options using different timing profiles with recommendations. The next section 7 describes the different network models, synchronization budgeting, right use of class of devices for both boundary and grandmaster clocks, solution guidelines for network operations including holdover, redundancy etc. The section 8 describes about timing solution and use cases, redundancy and resiliency network models. The annex section describes other technology aspects like, Microwave,
trace: 3 Scope

* Annex H updates:  
  * o Section H.3.3 has been newly introduced to define the Dynamic Analysis Requirements.
  * o Section H.3.2 has been restructured to clearly distinguish between PTP and SyncPhy static analysis requirements.
  * o Additional static analysis requirements have been incorporated into Section H.3.2.
  * o The font size across the entire Annex H has been standardized to 12pt for consistency.
  * o Tables H.4-1 and H.4-2 have been split into sub-tables A and B, representing PTP and SyncPhy dataset members, respectively.
  * o New tables H.4-1B and H.4-2B have been added to document SyncPhy dataset members.
  * o All static and dynamic analysis requirements have been revised to include normative language \(e.g., use of "shall"\) where applicable, to ensure clarity and enforceability.

  * 7 6.1.1.1 Synchronous Ethernet Clock
  * 8 Synchronous Ethernet Clock is also referred as Ethernet Equipment Clock \(EEC\). The ITU-T 
    * standard G.8262 \[14\] specification defines both synchronous Ethernet Equipment Clock \(EEC\) and

The first option, referred to as "Option 1", applies to synchronous equipment designed to interwork with networks optimized for the 2048 kbits/s hierarchy. text: with verification to Coordinated Universal Time \(UTC\). PRCs are typically built using Caesium

text: The main function of a PRTC, as defined in ITU-T G8272.1 amd1, is to deliver a primary time reference to be used in time and/or phase synchronization by other clocks of the network.

text: The PRTC takes its reference signal from a system connected to a recognized primary time standard \(e.g., a global navigation satellite system or from a national laboratory participating in time standards generation\). It can also optionally take a frequency input reference traceable to a PRC to maintain the local representation of the timescale during outages of the input time reference \(i.e., extend the phase/time holdover period of the clock\).
trace: 2 6 Network Timing and Synchronization Technology Overview --> 3 6.1 Building blocks of network-based synchronization -->
2 6 Network Timing and Synchronization Technology Overview --> 3 6.1 Building blocks of network-based synchronization -->

text: The performance of a GNSS-based PRTC can be impacted by several errors and one of the major sources of error is the ionospheric delay. The ionosphere introduces a variable time delay in the propagation of signals from the satellite to the receiver. The use of multi-constellation GNSS receivers is key to mitigate ionosphere effects and improve time accuracy. There are currently 6 GNSS satellite constellations in orbit providing geolocation and time distribution \(GPS, GLONASS, BeiDou, Galileo, Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System-IRNSS, Quasi-Zenith Satellite System-QZSS\). A multi-constellation GNSS increases the number of satellites in the view, which help mitigate issues linked to obstructions \(e.g., foliage, buildings, etc\) and provide additional redundancy and robustness of the system.
trace: 2 6 Network Timing and Synchronization Technology Overview --> 3 6.1 Building blocks of network-based synchronization -->
2 6 Network Timing and Synchronization Technology Overview --> 3 6.1 Building blocks of network-based synchronization -->

text: The low GNSS signal power on Earth makes it very susceptible to interference from weather and other signals. Over the past years, an increasing number of GNSS jamming, and spoofing have been reported. A small jammer can disrupt a GNSS receiver for several kilometres. GNSS jamming is a relatively simple technique that consists of producing an RF signal strong enough to interfere with the GNSS signal. GNSS jamming is a continuing threat and GNSS jamming devices have proliferated on the Internet.
trace: 2 6 Network Timing and Synchronization Technology Overview --> 3 6.1 Building blocks of network-based synchronization -->
2 6 Network Timing and Synchronization Technology Overview --> 3 6.1 Building blocks of network-based synchronization -->

text: GNSS spoofing is another threat more insidious and harder to detect. It consists of sending a false signal with a false position fix, a false clock offset, or both that the receiver interprets as the authentic GNSS signal.
trace: 2 6 Network Timing and Synchronization Technology Overview --> 3 6.1 Building blocks of network-based synchronization -->

text: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has declared the GPS "a single point of failure for critical infrastructure." \[36\]

text: The performance of the PRTC is characterized by two noise generation aspects:
trace: 2 6 Network Timing and Synchronization Technology Overview --> 3 6.1 Building blocks of network-based synchronization -->

trace: 2 6 Network Timing and Synchronization Technology Overview --> 3 6.1 Building blocks of network-based synchronization -->

text: • the amount of phase error \(wander and jitter\) produced at its output. The phase error is measured using the calculation of the maximum time interval error \(MTIE\) and the time deviation \(TDEV\) performance metrics.

text: When a PRTC+T-GM loses its input phase and time references, it enters the phase/time holdover state where it relies on the holdover of a local oscillator, or on an optional external input frequency reference traceable to a primary reference clock \(PRC\), or both. The quality of the local oscillator is an important feature. An OCXO oscillator can for example drift 400 ns in 8 hours while it takes a 1.8 day for a Rubidium oscillator to drift 400 ns. Note that the NR-TDD time error requirement with respect to a common reference is 1.5 s. Rubidium oscillator provides a 3-30x improvement over best aging XO spec \(0.01ppd/day\). Rubidium oscillators are typically deployed to in PRTC+T-GM locations where there is a need to offer an additional level of protection with a better holdover period when no other mechanism is available.

text: ITU-T G.8272.1 \[37\] specifies that under normal, locked operating conditions, the time output of the ePRTC- or the combined ePRTC and T-GM function, should be accurate to within 30 ns or better when verified against the applicable primary time standard \(e.g., UTC\).

text: When an ePRTC loses all its input phase and time references and enters the phase/time holdover state, it relies on an autonomous primary reference clock \(PRC\) frequency reference input. An ePRTC can also rely on several input frequency references used to ensemble a very stable frequency reference. An ePRTC is an autonomous source of time and independent timescale that is implemented with one or two co-located atomic clocks.
trace: 2 6 Network Timing and Synchronization Technology Overview --> 3 6.1 Building blocks of network-based synchronization -->

text: The holdover requirements of an ePRTC-A when verified against the applicable primary time standard \(e.g., UTC\) is defined from the start of phase/time holdover, after 30 days of continuous normal operation, to within a value increasing linearly from 30 ns to 100 ns over a 14-day period \(see Table and Figure below\). ePRTCs are typically deployed in major timing centres in order to provide a long holdover capability. ePRTCs are extremely reliable clock immune to jamming and spoofing given their high level of autonomy.

text: Assisted partial timing support \(APTS\) offers a backup timing source to GNSS-based inter-working function \(IWF P-F\) \[38\].

text: The latter serves as the primary synchronization source for the full timing support network in the access network. APTS typically uses a secondary synchronization source from the partial timing support network in the pre-aggregation/aggregation network as a backup mechanism provided that the full timing support time error budget remains in relatively small \(e.g., two or three hops\).
trace: 2 6 Network Timing and Synchronization Technology Overview --> 3 6.1 Building blocks of network-based synchronization --> 6.1.4 APTS

text: In normal mode of operation, the time of the GNSS-based IWF time is sourced from GNSS, and in the event of GNSS loss, it relies on the frequency derived from the incoming PTP flow of the partial timing support network to provide or hold time. Note that alternatively, it is possible to use a traceable frequency input \(e.g., SyncE, 2 048 kHz interfaces, 1 544 kbit/s interfaces, 2 048 kbit/s interfaces, etc\) from a local frequency source.

text: 6.2 Timing profiles
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles

text:
* Timing profile specifies the IEEE 1588 functions that are necessary to ensure network element interoperability
  * for the delivery of accurate phase/time synchronization.
  * 6.2.1 Full Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.1\)
  * ITU-T G.8275.1 \[1\] specifies a profile for telecommunication applications based on IEEE 1588 precision time
  * protocol \(PTP\). The profile specifies the IEEE 1588 functions that are necessary to ensure network element
  * interoperability for the delivery of accurate phase/time synchronization. The profile is based on the full timing
  * support from the network architecture as described in ITU-T G.8275 \[41\] and definitions described in ITU-T
  * G.8260 \[17\].
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles
6.2 Timing profiles
6.2 Timing profiles

text:
* This version of the profile specifies the high-level design requirements, modes of operation for the exchange
  * of PTP messages, the PTP protocol mapping, the best timeTransmitter clock algorithm \(BTCA\) options, as
  * well as the PTP protocol configuration parameters.
  * Note-1 − The parameters defined in this version of the specification are chosen based on the case where
  * physical layer frequency support is provided, and the case without physical layer frequency support \(i.e., PTP
  * only\) is for further study
  * Reco – This specification restricts the usage of IEEE1588 version 2.0 \[20\] only. It does not include the 
  * IEEE1588 version 2.1, and this version will be considered in the future.
  * As per this profile every network node between Grand Master device and end-application is PTP and Sync-E
  * aware devices. It is referred as Full path Timing Support \(FTS\) profile.
  * The common accepted devices are Telecom Boundary Clock \(T-BC\) and Telecom Transparent Clock \(T-TC\)
  * for the nodes between GM and End-application.

text: 6.2.2 Partial Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.2\)
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles --> 6.2.2 Partial Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.2\)

text: This profile is for telecommunication applications based on \[IEEE 1588\] precision time protocol \(PTP\). The profile specifies the IEEE 1588 functions that are necessary to ensure network element interoperability for the delivery of accurate phase/time \(and frequency\) synchronization with partial timing support from network and commonly referred as PTS profile.
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles --> 6.2.2 Partial Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.2\)

text: This profile defines the PTP profile for unicast mode only.
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles --> 6.2.2 Partial Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.2\)

text: Figure 6.2.2-1: Partial Timing Support network model
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles --> 6.2.2 Partial Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.2\) --> Figure 6.2.2-1: Partial Timing Support network model

text: The clock specifications for T-BC-P and T-TSC-P are defined in ITU-T G.8273.4 \[39\] standard. In a Partial Timing Support \(PTS\) model, some or all nodes between the Grandmaster and End time-synchronous clock \(T-TSC\) are not aware of PTP. As in Figure 6.2.2-1 above, the T-GM and T-BC-P is connected over a network \(that may contain one or multiple network nodes\) that do not support PTP.
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles --> 6.2.2 Partial Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.2\)

text: The term telecom boundary clock for partial timing support \(T-BC-P\) refers to a device consisting of a boundary clock \(BC\) as defined in \[IEEE 1588\], with additional performance characteristics as defined in ITU-T G.8273.4 \[39\].
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles --> 6.2.2 Partial Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.2\)

text: The term telecom time synchronous clock for partial timing support \(T-TSC-P\) refers to a device consisting of either an ordinary clock \(OC\), with one PTP port, or a boundary clock \(BC\), with multiple PTP ports, as defined in \[IEEE 1588\] and with additional performance characteristics as defined in ITU-T G.8273.4 \[39\].
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles --> 6.2.2 Partial Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.2\)

text: The IWF stands for Inter Working Function. In this network model the IWF boundary clock exercises G.8275.2 \[3\] \(Partial timing support\) profile towards the network Grand Master side and G.8275.1 \[1\] \(Full timing support\) profile towards the O-RU/T-TSC.
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles --> 6.2.2 Partial Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.2\)

text: The network operating in partial timing support may not be sufficient to meet all of the applicable timing requirements. See Appendix II in G.8271.2 \[9\] on Considerations for handling precision time protocol traffic in networks with partial timing support. One important aspect is that this methodology requires manual compensation for asymmetries at installation and at any change in the network. This is particularly critical when the transport technology can introduce variable asymmetries \(e.g., at restart of an equipment\).
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles --> 6.2.2 Partial Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.2\)

text: The use of G.8275.2 \[3\] in partial timing support is for further study in the CUS \[33\] specification, in particular, the following is stated in the CUS specification \(ref.12\): "Transport of PTP directly over L2 Ethernet \(ITU-T G.8275.1 \[1\] full timing on-path support\) is assumed in this version of the specification, whilst transport of PTP over UDP/IP \(ITU-T G.8275.2 \[3\] partial timing support from the network\) is also possible albeit with unassured synchronization performance."
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles --> 6.2.2 Partial Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.2\)

text: It should be noted that if the cluster of base stations is synchronized via a full timing support segment \(i.e., after the IWF\), the impact from the partial timing support segment of the network on timing requirements related to coordination features such as carrier aggregation, is negligible.
trace: 6.2 Timing profiles --> 6.2.2 Partial Timing Support \(ITU-T G.8275.2\)

text: Reco: ITU-T G.8275.2 \[3\] standard allows both PTPoIPv4 and PTPoIPv6 unicast transport mechanisms, this ORAN specification recommends using PTPoIPv4. Usage of PTPoIPv6 is FFS.

text: Similar considerations as indicated above may apply for the periods during which the GNSS is lost and PTP becomes the synchronization timeTransmitter for the O-RU. However, differently from the previous case, APTS allows for automatic removal of static asymmetries when PTP is used.

text: 6.3.1 Factors to be considered for network synchronization budgeting
trace: 6.3 Synchronization time error budgeting model --> 6.3.1 Factors to be considered for network synchronization budgeting

text: 6.3.1.1 SyncE/Physical layer clock switchover and phase transient
trace: 6.3 Synchronization time error budgeting model --> 6.3.1.1 SyncE/Physical layer clock switchover and phase transient

text:
* A rearrangement of the PHY frequency \(Sync-E\) results in the phase/time error at each T-BC, the T-TSC and the end application.
  * The TE is generally larger in the congruent scenario than in the non-congruent scenario because in the congruent scenario each T-BC has errors due to the re-arrangement transient in both time and frequency planes.
  * The frequency plane error is due to PHY frequency input and time/phase error due to PTP sync messages input to a T-BC from the upstream T-BC.
  * Refer Figure II.3 for congruent scenario and II.4 for non-congruent scenario in ITU-T G.8271.1 \[8\] standard.
  * Refer ITU-T G.8271.1 Appendix-V1: Mitigation of time error due to synchronous ethernet transients.
  * Refer ITU-T G.8273.2 \[2\] Annex-B: Control of the phase transient due to rearrangements in the synchronous ethernet network

text: E. PTP Hybrid \(PTP + SyncE/eSyncE\) network:
trace: 6.3 Synchronization time error budgeting model --> E. PTP Hybrid \(PTP + SyncE/eSyncE\) network:

text: In order to have accurate and stable S-Plane on O-RUs, it is recommended to have PTP and SyncE/eSyncE for Phase/Time and Frequency recovery on O-RU for achieving better time error accuracy\(absolute/relative\) at the outputs of O-RUs. It is also recommended to have the O-RU equipped with better jitter/wander filtering capabilities to keep the noise especially at lower frequencies as low as possible. In otherwords, if SyncE is used, the O-RU must have appropriate low pass filtering to reject SyncE jitter, and if not used then O-RU must implement a stable local oscillator.

trace: A. Shorter chain of Clocks: --> B. Clock source redundancy: --> 6.3.1.3 Class of devices and time errors

text: The noise generation of a T-GM/T-BC and a T-TSC represents the amount of noise produced at the output of the T-GM/T-BC/T-TSC when there is an ideal input reference packet timing signal. Under normal, locked operating conditions, the time output of the T-BC and the T-TSC should be accurate to within the maximum absolute time error \(TE\) \(max|TE|\). This value includes all the noise components, i.e., the constant time error \(cTE\) and the dynamic time error \(dTE\) noise generation.

text: 6.3.2.1 General Budgeting model

text: When time error budget is calculated there are three different aspects to that:
trace: 6.3.2 Time Error budget calculation --> 6.3.2.1 General Budgeting model

text:
* 1\. Time Error from Time source \(Ex. T-GM\) to O-RU \(Input to O-RU and up until Radio Interface\)
  * 2\. Time Error from Time source \(Ex: T-GM\) to O-DU
  * 3\. Time Error between O-RU to O-RU radio interfaces Also called as Relative Time Alignment Error \(TAE\).
trace: 6.3.2 Time Error budget calculation --> 6.3.2.1 General Budgeting model
6.3.2 Time Error budget calculation --> 6.3.2.1 General Budgeting model

text: For each type described above one needs to start with overall time error budget as the end number to start with and calculate back by subtracting the individual budgets for each of the following that are applicable:
trace: 6.3.2 Time Error budget calculation --> 6.3.2.1 General Budgeting model

text:
* 1\. Half of asymmetry \(caused by Network, Fiber, Wavelength used or Optics\)
  * 2\. Holdover budget \(for Radio, Network nodes, GM or combination of these\)
  * 3\. Number of hops and cTE and dTEL of each of the network nodes based on clock types and time error of T-GM/PRTC based on PRTC type.
  * 4\. Sync-E/Physical layer clock switchover phase error
trace: 6.3.2 Time Error budget calculation --> 6.3.2.1 General Budgeting model
6.3.2 Time Error budget calculation --> 6.3.2.1 General Budgeting model

text:
* For example:
  * T : Target Time Error budget \(Ex. 1.5 microseconds for TDD network\)
  * T\(g\) : time error of PRTC+GM
  * T\(n\) : time error for all network nodes \(boundary clocks\)
  * T\(r\) : time error of Radio device
  * T\(h\) : holdover timer error budget
  * T\(a\) : time error budget for asymmetry
  * T\(s\) : time error budget for SyncE re-arrangement.
  * T\(c\) : Total calculated time error budget
trace: 6.3.2 Time Error budget calculation --> 6.3.2.1 General Budgeting model

text: 7.1 Factors to be considered for synchronization network design
trace: --> 7.1 Factors to be considered for synchronization network design

text: 7.1.1 Source of clock and location of clock source
trace: --> 7.1 Factors to be considered for synchronization network design --> 7.1.1 Source of clock and location of clock source

text:
* The source of timing should be traceable to a recognized primary time standard such as the Coordinated Universal Time \(UTC\) or a global navigation satellite system \(GNSS\). The GNSS time offset from UTC is contained in the GNSS broadcast message. UTC is the international reference time that is computed by the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures \(BIPM\) from hundreds of atomic clocks maintained in national laboratories worldwide. Local representations of UTC, commonly called UTC\(k\) time scales, are maintained by national measurement institutes and time
  * laboratories. GNSS uses a constellation of low-orbit satellites that covers the entire Earth's surface. 
  * It should be noted that for the purpose of meeting the 3GPP synchronization requirements \(e.g., CPS\), there is no need to recover UTC time even when UTC traceability is required.
  * ePRTCs are typically distributed in the 5G Core location to protect their timing networks against regional GNSS and global GNSS outages. An ePRTC system provides in the core of the network an independent and autonomous timescale aligned with GNSS to deliver both frequency, phase and time.
  * PRTCs are typically deployed in a CRAN Hub location where they distribute timing to the Boundary Clocks and O-DUs. The PRTCs can also, in an APTS configuration, receive timing from other PRTCs further down in the pre-aggregation/aggregation network.
trace: --> 7.1 Factors to be considered for synchronization network design --> 7.1.1 Source of clock and location of clock source

text: 7.1.2 GM/clock source resiliency
trace: --> 7.1.2 GM/clock source resiliency

text: Timing is a mission critical service that needs to be protected by designing a highly available timing infrastructure so that no failure will cause the timing service to become unavailable. The timing infrastructure is typically dependent upon GNSS as the timing source. The latter is a single point of failure if the GNSS signal is jammed or spoofed at the PRTC-B location \(e.g., Central Office, Mobile Telephone Switching Office -MTSO, etc\). It is important to take appropriate measures to mitigate the risks against GNSS failure.
trace: --> 7.1.2 GM/clock source resiliency

text: Several mechanisms of resiliency can be implemented to ensure the continuity of the timing service:
trace: --> 7.1.2 GM/clock source resiliency

text:
* multi-constellation GNSS to protect against one constellation failure.
  * GNSS Anti-jamming/spoofing on the PRTC-B GNSS antenna \(GNSS failure\)
  * e-PRTC-A to provide up to 14-days of holdover while maintaining up to 100 ns of accuracy.
  * PRTC-B equipped with Rubidium oscillator to extend the holdover period.
  * Alternate BTCA \(PRTC/T-GM failure\) for the timing network to automatically select an alternate PRTC-B in a different location.
  * High Availability PRTC/T-GM to automatically transfer the IP address of the PRTC-B to another one in a different building.

text: The topology shown in Figure 7.1.6-1, has boundary clocks R1 to R7 and each boundary clock is serving one or more RUs or Base stations. In normal operation condition R1 recovers time from GM and drives to both R2 and R7 nodes in downstream. RU1 connected to R7 is two hops away from GM \(R1 and R7\) shown as green dotted line above. In this normal operational condition, the end-to-end time error budget for RU1 is just two hops away from GM.

If the link between R1 and R7 goes down, the same RU1 would have to recover the clock over longest chain of nodes \(R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6 and R7\) as shown in red dotted line. It is important to plan and design the network by calculating the time-error budget for the longest synchronization path rather than shortest or best path possible. Otherwise, synchronization does not work in network failure condition.

text: What is asymmetry?
trace: -->  --> What is asymmetry?

text:
* Difference in propagation delay between the forward and reverse path of PTP timeReceiver node from its upstream timeTransmitter node.
  * Half of uncorrected asymmetry would translate to time error offset in the packet timeReceiver clock from its timeTransmitter clock.

* Static asymmetry The \(propagation\) delay is constant or remains same irrespective of reboot of the node/optics or system.
  * Dynamic \(or semi static\) asymmetry The delay is not constant, or it would vary from reboot or reset of the node or interface or optics module.

Effective asymmetry introduced is 50 x 4.9 = 225 ns. Half of asymmetry would translate to time-error offset recovered at timeReceiver node, 225/2 => 122.5 ns at timeReceiver clock \(R2\). The
trace: -->  --> 7.1.7.1.1 Link/Fiber asymmetry

Half of this asymmetry \(490/2 => 245 ns\) would translate into time-error offset at timeReceiver clock.

trace: -->  --> 7.1.7.1.2 Asymmetry in optics \(Grey optics\)

text: The propagation delay inside the optics module is not zero. Especially the Tx and Rx may not be equal within a given optics. This introduces static asymmetry within the optics. This is typically seen as small value unlike the fiber asymmetry, but every nanosecond counts for high precision sync requirement.
trace: -->  --> 7.1.7.1.2 Asymmetry in optics \(Grey optics\)

text: 7.1.7.1.3 Wavelength Asymmetry
trace: -->  --> 7.1.7.1.3 Wavelength Asymmetry

text: The asymmetry due to the use of different wavelength is obtained by calculating the group delay applicable to wavelengths used in the forward and in the reverse direction.
trace: -->  --> 7.1.7.1.3 Wavelength Asymmetry

text: Asymmetry A = df – dr = L \* \(nr – nf\)/c
trace: -->  --> 7.1.7.1.3 Wavelength Asymmetry

text:
* L is the distance \(fiber length\)
  * c is the speed of light.
  * df and dr are the forward and reverse transmission delay.
  * nr and nf are the group refractive indexes applicable at the wavelength used in the forward and reverse direction, respectively.
trace: -->  --> 7.1.7.1.3 Wavelength Asymmetry

text: The evaluation of the refractive indexes can be done either using known chromatic dispersion data \(e.g., from the optical fiber data sheet\) or, in the case that the dispersion is unknown, making a direct delay measurement at three different wavelengths \(the refractive index for an arbitrary wavelength can then be derived by quadratic interpolation\).
trace: -->  --> 7.1.7.1.3 Wavelength Asymmetry
-->  --> 7.1.7.1.3 Wavelength Asymmetry
-->  --> 7.1.7.1.3 Wavelength Asymmetry
-->  --> 7.1.7.1.3 Wavelength Asymmetry

text: These data can then be used to derive the group delay of a generic wavelength. In particular, in the case of an ITU-T G.652 compliant fiber, the group delay at the applicable wavelengths can be calculated making use of the Sellmeier equations as described in ITU-T G.652 standard.
Note: For additional details refer Appendix-III in ITU-T G.8271 \[7\] standard and group delay specification and measurement method are specified in G.671 \[40\], Clause 3.2.2.25.

text: 7.1.9 Selection of timing profile
trace: --> 7.1.8 PTP packet transport --> 7.1.9 Selection of timing profile

text: In general profile selection is driven based on following criteria:
trace: --> 7.1.8 PTP packet transport --> 7.1.9 Selection of timing profile

text:
* Target Synchronization Precision requirement
  * o The target precision requirement plays critical role in selection of timing profile.
  * o For high precise application \(+/-130 nsec\), ITU-T G.8275.1 \[1\] profile is recommended.
  * o For end to end 1.5usec target it may be possible to achieve using ITU-T G.8275.2 \[3\] profile with proper planning and budgeting.
  * o Additionally, FFO limits must be considered.
  * Transport mechanism used in the transport network.
  * o The usage of L3 versus L2 protocols in the transport nodes sometimes lead to selection of profile as G.8275.1 \[1\] \(L2\) or G.8275.2 \(L3\) \[3\].
  * o The end nodes capability to support the specific timing profile will also play an important role in selecting timing for profile for the transport network nodes.
  * The sync capability of the network nodes used in the transport.
  * o The capability of every node supporting synchronization in the transport network can be a factor in deciding the right profile.
  * o In green field network it is possible to use full timing support profile \(G.8275.1 \[1\]\) but in brown field network it might be possible with G.8275.2 \[3\] profile.
  * Access to GNSS at cell site and associated CapEx and OpEx leverage
  * o Sync can be delivered directly or close to the base-station nodes based on the accessibility and availability of GNSS either at cell site or close to the cell-site.
  * o When associated cost is not a bigger concern for installation and maintenance of the high number of GNSS/T-GMs in the network.
  * Network hops in the sync network
  * o In some cases, it may be practically limiting to achieve the targeted sync precision if too many network hops between the T-GM and O-RU \(base station nodes\).
  * o This can lead to usage of LLS-C4 option with GNSS directly connected to base-station.
  * Asymmetry and control over asymmetry in the network
  * o If asymmetry \(packet, path, link asymmetry\) expected to be difficult to control, choosing right profile would play a critical role.
  * o For example full timing support profile gives better control to address the network asymmetry than partial timing support profiles.
  * Administrator control of the synchronization network path
  * o Any network hops/cloud\(s\) in the middle of synchronization path that does not belong to mobile operator administrative control can be risky to deploy sync.
  * o Example if mobile operator selects full timing support profile, and intermediate cloud/network provider does not support timing in their network, it will break the synchronization chain.
trace: --> 7.1.8 PTP packet transport --> 7.1.9 Selection of timing profile

text: Reco: This ORAN specification recommends G.8275.1 \[1\] full timing support profile and hence plan for the transport network to accommodate the transport mechanism described in this  profile \(PTP over Ethernet Multicast\).

text: In this model, T-GM is located deep in the network \(core or edge of the network\). All nodes from GM to base station nodes are aware of timing and capable of supporting T-BC clock as per G.8273.2 \[2\] standard using full timing support profile \(G.8275.1 \[1\]\).

text: Advantages of this deployment model:
trace: --> 7.2 GM deployment models --> 7.2.1 Centralized GM network model

text:
* Don't need to deploy and manage high number of PRTC/T-GM clocks in the network as the clock sync flows from core of the network.
  * OpEx and CapEx will be low as fewer T-GMs are needed.
  * No constraints on GNSS line of sight access issue at cell-sites

text: 7.2.4 Comparison of Centralized versus Distributed GM network model
trace: --> 7.2.2 Distributed GM network model --> 7.2.4 Comparison of Centralized versus Distributed GM network model

text: This section describes the disadvantages of distributed and network-based sync models:
trace: --> 7.2.2 Distributed GM network model --> 7.2.4 Comparison of Centralized versus Distributed GM network model
--> 7.2.2 Distributed GM network model --> 7.2.4 Comparison of Centralized versus Distributed GM network model

text: Direct GNSS to Base station:
trace: --> 7.2.2 Distributed GM network model --> 7.2.4 Comparison of Centralized versus Distributed GM network model --> Direct GNSS to Base station:

text:
* Single point of failure
  * Line of sight access to GNSS can be an issue if it is urban deployment.
  * Jamming and/or spoofing can bring down the entire cell site down.
  * No extended holdover possible as it depends on oscillator used in the base-station nodes.
  * High precision sync application that needs precision between the cluster of cell-sites to be precise with less than or equal to +/-130 or +/-65 nanoseconds \(ex: Carrier aggregation, NR MIMO, LTE MIMO\) may not be achievable with direct GNSS based sync.
  * Ex1: PRTC-A it is difficult to achieve even +/-130 nsec even with enhanced Radio.
  * Ex2: PRTC-B it is difficult to achieve +/-65 nsec even with enhanced Radio.
  * OpEx and CapEx may be high as it depends on how many base stations deployed.
  * Cost of monitoring and downtime is high.
trace: --> 7.2.2 Distributed GM network model --> 7.2.4 Comparison of Centralized versus Distributed GM network model --> Direct GNSS to Base station:

  * Asymmetry in the network can cause time/phase recovery error.
  * Any node behaves incorrectly in the chain of nodes from GM to base-station, can affect entire chain of downstream nodes performance.
  * KPI can be complex in wholesale environment especially with G.8275.2 \[3\] profile deployment case.

text: 8 Timing Use cases and Solution Options
trace: --> 8 Timing Use cases and Solution Options

text: This section describes the timing and synchronization solution options when applied to actual deployment use cases provided by operators. The main synchronization objective is to synchronize the radios with their serving O-DUs and maintain required timing performance \(absolute between O-RU and O-DU, and relative between O-RUs\).
trace: --> 8 Timing Use cases and Solution Options
--> 8 Timing Use cases and Solution Options

text: 8.1 Transport network topology
trace: --> 8.1 Transport network topology

text: Based on the operator use cases provided in \[32\], more detailed transport network topology, particularly related to the Access Transport Network, is described in the following subsections.
trace: --> 8.1 Transport network topology
--> 8.1 Transport network topology

text: The icons of network transport nodes used in the diagram are defined as follows:
trace: --> 8.1 Transport network topology

text:
* CSR: Cell Site Router, collocated with O-RUs
  * HSR: Hub Site Router, aggregation router with large switching capacity
  * HSR-F: Hub Site Router that distribute fronthaul traffics to O-DUs
  * HSR-B/M: Hub Site Router that aggregate Backhaul or Midhaul traffics.
trace: --> 8.1 Transport network topology
--> 8.1 Transport network topology

text: 8.1.1 C-RAN Architecture with non-collocated O-RU and O-DU
trace: --> 8.1 Transport network topology --> 8.1.1 C-RAN Architecture with non-collocated O-RU and O-DU

text: Figure 8.1.1-1 presents a Hub-Spoke topology that is applied to the Access Transport Network for the operator use case Scenario 1 in \[32\], where O-RUs are located at cell site and O-DUs and O-CUs are collocated at the Hub site. The topology is described as follows:
trace: --> 8.1 Transport network topology --> 8.1.1 C-RAN Architecture with non-collocated O-RU and O-DU

text:
* The CSR aggregates the fronthaul traffics from multiple O-RUs in the same site and transports the merged traffic via high-speed ports to the Hub.
  * The HSR aggregates the Fronthaul traffic from multiple sites.
  * The HSR-F distributes the Fronthaul traffic received from HSR to the serving O-DUs that are paired to the corresponding O-RUs.
  * O-DU and O-CU are connected internally without going through transport network, or they are implemented as an integrated unit.
  * The backhaul traffic from the multiple O-CUs are aggregated by HSR-H and are transported to the aggregation Transport network.
  * Connection between HSR and HSR-B is established for management and/or synchronization purposes.
  * Optionally, the HSR-F may not be used and O-DUs are directly connected to HSR.

* Maintain the frequency and time/phase synchronization between O-RU and its serving O-DU, within the specified Timing Alignment Error \(TAE\) allowance.
  * Maintain the frequency and time/phase synchronization between O-RUs that are connected to the same CSR, within the specified Timing Alignment Error \(TAE\) allowance, per 3GPP Timing Precision requirement for different wireless applications.
  * Maintain the frequency and time/phase synchronization between O-RUs that are not connected to the same CSR, within the specified Timing Alignment Error \(TAE\) allowance, per 3GPP Timing Precision requirement for different wireless applications.

text: 8.1.2 C-RAN Architecture with O-RU and O-DU collocated at cell site
trace: --> 8.1 Transport network topology --> 8.1.2 C-RAN Architecture with O-RU and O-DU collocated at cell site

text: This use case applies to the Hub-spoke architecture to Operator use case scenario 2, as shown in Figure 8.1.2-1, where O-DU and O-RU are collocated at the cell site, and O-CUs are centralized at the Hub site. The transport traffics flow is summarized as follows:
trace: --> 8.1 Transport network topology --> 8.1.2 C-RAN Architecture with O-RU and O-DU collocated at cell site

text:
* The O-RUs are connected to O-DUs via the Fronthaul link going through the CSR in the same site.
  * The CSR also aggregates the Midhaul traffic from multiple O-DUs in the same site and transports the merged traffic to the Hub.
  * There are two logical flows \(Fronthaul, Midhaul\) between O-DU and CSR as shown in the Figure 8.1.2-1.
  * The HSR aggregates the Midhaul traffics from multiple cells sites.
  * The backhaul traffics from the multiple O-CUs are aggregated by HSR-B and are transported to the Aggregation Transport network.
  * Connection between HSR and HSR-B is established for management or synchronization purposes.

text: For the transport network with larger scale that need to facilitate multiple O-DUs, the LLS-C2 timing solution is implemented as shown in Figure 8.2.1-9, where a single HSR router is used for traffic aggregation and providing switching flexibility among O-DUs. The T-GM distributes the PTP timing to the O-DUs directly.
trace: --> 8.2.1 Timing Solutions for C-RAN Architecture with non-collocated O-RU and O-DU --> 8.2.1.8 Timing Solution for LLS-C2 configuration with multiple O-DUs

text: Since the HSR is only allowed to lock to a single timing source by the definition of the G8275.1 profile, only one O-DU \(denoted as the primary O-DU\) is active in the PTP path. This primary O- DU may control the timing of multiple cell sites that are directly connected to the HSR. The rest of O-DUs are effectively acts as backup time source in this use case scenario.
trace: --> 8.2.1 Timing Solutions for C-RAN Architecture with non-collocated O-RU and O-DU --> 8.2.1.8 Timing Solution for LLS-C2 configuration with multiple O-DUs

text: It is evident that the Primary O-DU and HSR-F that provide the PTP path are single point of failure. To improve the redundancy, the PTP functions in all O-DUs are enabled to deliver multiple PTP flows simultaneously to next hop node, even though only one of them is used by HSR. In the event of any failure, the A-BTCA function at next hop is responsible to detect the failover and automatically select and switch over to alternative PTP flow.

text: 8.2.4.2 General Resiliency Solutions
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.2 General Resiliency Solutions

text: The following resiliency implementation is recommended for a reliable timing/sync architecture:
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.2 General Resiliency Solutions

text:
* Dual timing sources \(T-GMs\)
  * Duplicated TNEs that may have large scale of impact the \(HSRs, HSR-Bs, etc.\)
  * Dual connectivity/Dual homing \(T-GM to TNE, TNE to TNE, TNE to O-DU\)
  * Enable standby PTP in all resilience devices.
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.2 General Resiliency Solutions

text: Note: During synchronization network failover condition, with certain combination of clock types \(specifically with large number of hops\), Sync-E transient and/or PTP re-arrangement may cause short-term degradation in performance and that might affect the operation of the radio interface \(particularly, the frequency stability requirement on the radio interface might be impacted\).
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.2 General Resiliency Solutions

text: 8.2.4.2.1 PTP Resiliency
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.2.1 PTP Resiliency

text: As part of resiliency network model, there will be multiple PTP paths available. Only one of the paths for a timeReceiver node will be selected for primary operation of the G8275.1 profile and rest are considered as the standby that are used only if failure occurs. This is illustrated in the figure below, where the active PTP \(blue arrow\) indicates the PTP that is sent to the node and it is used to synchronize its clock while the standby PTP \(grey arrow\) indicates the PTP that is sent to the node but it is not taken as source of synchronization until a failover occurs.

text: Figure 8.2.4-4 Resiliency solution
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul -->  --> Figure 8.2.4-4 Resiliency solution

text: Selection of the primary \(active\) PTP path or switchover to alternate path when failure occurs is controlled by A-BTCA algorithm that will be driven by the different PTP attributes configured on those nodes:
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul -->

text:
* Local priority settings to facilitate pre-determined PTP path.
  * Timing performance \(clock accuracy or clock variance\) based switchover.
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul -->

text: The goal of the resiliency design is to minimize the disruption whenever PTP path changes:
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul -->

text:
* Maintain the same time source \(T-GM\) as much as possible.
  * Maintain same timing topology \(number of nodes/clocks, number of hops\) as much as possible.
  * Minimize changes in the PTP path.
  * Sync-E sourced from the same time source as the PTP source \(T-GM\) is recommended.
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul -->

text: 8.2.4.2.2 Resiliency under LAG
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.2.2 Resiliency under LAG

text: In case of multiple links between two nodes configured, such as LAG bundle, PTP can be enabled on more than one links. In the event when one link fails, A-BTCA can automatically switchover to another link under the LAG bundle. Local priority can be configured such that the A-BTCA picks the link from the same LAG bundle than the link connected to another node, as shown in Figure  8.2.4-5. \(The circle indicates LAG bundle in the figure\)

text: 8.2.4.2.3 Sync-E Configuration
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.2.3 Sync-E Configuration

text: As part of G8275.1 profile, Sync-E shall also be enabled along the path from the timing source \(T- GM\) to the end application node \(T-TSC\). The Sync-E is hop-by-hop service, therefore each node along the path shall be configured.
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.2.3 Sync-E Configuration

text: Sync-E source selection or switching is not controlled by PTP A-BTCA, rather it can be achieved via configuration, based on separate priority and clock quality level. Hence the Sync-E path may choose different links from the PTP when failover occurs. Note that dual/redundancy timing source case model, it is preferred that the Sync-E and PTP always driven from the same PRTC/T-GM, even though they may take different network paths or optionally Sync-E can be on the same path as the PTP so that both can switch simultaneously.

text: Note that whenever the PTP path changes, there is possible impact on the timing performance. For example, the first case in the above when the link from HSR A to a CSR fails, the relative timing accuracy between inter site O-RUs will degrade because the nearest common BC is extended to T- GM A. One option to maintain the same timing performance is to choose to use HSR B for all cell sites.
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> O-RAN.WG9.XTRP-SYN.0-R004-v07.00

text: Note: Clock distribution in the Xhaul networks is recommended \(depending on the topology\) to be uni-directional from upstream to downstream \(Backhaul to Midhaul and Midhaul to Fronthaul\). When a clock flow changes from downstream to upstream \(also known as Clock backflow\), caused by a failure in a link or node, it is very difficult to predict the failed over clock flow, and it may cause unexpected deterioration of clock accuracy.

text: 8.2.4.4 ePRTC Resiliency
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.4 ePRTC Resiliency

text: High availability is one of the key requirements for 5G. It is important to design the 5G synchronization to be highly available with redundancy integrated at all levels of the synchronization infrastructure starting from the source of timing. The resiliency of the timing source is critical to achieve an overall goal of a survivable and fault tolerant synchronization infrastructure. It is essential that the timing infrastructure continues to maintain an acceptable level of service in the event of failures and faults affecting normal operations.
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.4 ePRTC Resiliency

text: There is a growing number of intentional and unintentional GNSS incidents. During such extended GNSS outages, ePRTC-A systems operating as an autonomous primary reference clocks can be deployed to maintain time and frequency service in a geographical area. ePRTC-A delivers a high- level of service reliability to ensure operators maintain an acceptable time and frequency service performance for a long period of GNSS unavailability. The frequency stability of a Cesium atomic clock serves as a reference for the ePRTC-A Time Scale.
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.4 ePRTC Resiliency

text: ePRTC-A offers the following features:
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.4 ePRTC Resiliency

text:
* Reliability: Immunity from local jamming or outages
  * Autonomy: Atomic clock sustained timescale with & without GNSS connection
  * Holdover: 14-day time holdover <= 100 ns
trace: --> 8.2.2.1 Timing Solution for LLS-C3 configuration with T-GM from Midhaul --> 8.2.4.4 ePRTC Resiliency

text: When an ePRTC-A loses all its input phase and time references, it enters the phase/time holdover state and relies on an autonomous primary frequency reference input \(e.g., 2MHz, 10MHz, etc.\) to deliver time and phase. This autonomous primary reference clock is typically a Cesium atomic clock. Refer Figure 8.2.4-19, for an ePRTC-A, from the start of phase/time holdover, after 30 days of continuous normal operation, the time output should be accurate, when verified against the applicable primary time standard \(e.g., UTC\), to within a value increasing linearly from 30 ns to 100 ns over a 14-day period.

text: The ePRTC-A systems are typically deployed in core and large hub sites to deliver a synchronization service to the smaller Hub sites and cell sites located in a local geographical area as shown in Figure  8.2.4-24. In the event of GNSS outage impacting that area, the ePRTC-A in a holdover state will be able to deliver an acceptable frequency and phase to the Hub and cell sites for up to 14 days.
Figure 8.2.4-24 : ePRTC-A deployment in core site

A fully redundant ePRTC-A system as shown in Figure 8.2.4-25 allows to protect against most types of failures. The back-up ePRTC-A unit equipped with its own antenna will provide protection against antenna failures, and software/hardware failures. The A-BTCA protocol can be used to select the best ePRTC-A clock. Alternatively, an IP failover mechanism between the two ePRTC-A units can constantly compare their health metrics and switch-over automatically from the active to the back-up unit if the health of the active one becomes degraded.

Diverse topology \(link and node\) design is essential to build a survivable network timing infrastructure that distributes time and frequency from the core and hub sites to the cell sites. It is important to protect the distribution of the timing information against link and node failures. The fully redundant ePRTC-A system is connected to the network via two different network access points located on separate physical nodes. A failure at one node or link should not disrupt the delivery of frequency and time/phase to the network.
The topology shown in Figure 8.2.4-25 illustrates the different types of failures that can be effectively handled using the fully redundant ePRTC-A system.

* Node failure \(failure 1\): The ePRTC-A is protected against a failure of the adjacent north side BC node, port or link by switching over to the south side port by A-BTCA.
  * Node failure \(failure 2\): One ePRTC-A node port failure is protected by another ePRTC-A node
  * Antenna failure \(failure 3\): One ePRTC-A is protected against an antenna failure by the selection of the standby ePRTC-A node.
  * ePRTC software/hardware failure \(failure 4\): The ePRTC-A node failure is protected by another ePRTC-A node.
Figure 8.2.4-25 : Fully redundant ePRTC-A deployment in large Hub site

text: A.3 Impact of interference
trace: --> A.3 Impact of interference

text: Like all radio communications systems, Point-to-Point \(PP\) and Point-to-Multiple-Point \(PMP\) microwave and mmWave radio transport links are susceptible to radio interference from adjacent and parallel links as well from other services, such as radar, Radio LAN and Short-Range devices, that could be sharing the band or operating in adjacent band to the radio transport fixed service. Communication failure may occur due to the influence of this interference, and the \(TE\) characteristics may deteriorate accordingly. The severity of TE degradation depends on the equipment and the techniques used to mitigate the impact of interference. As such the design and selection of the bands should take into considering TE degradation due to the external environment. Examples of considerations to mitigate the effect of interference, include avoiding the use of license exempt bands for time sensitive applications, use high quality antenna with very low side lobes \(e.g., ETSI Class 4\), and apply for high protection and availability link licenses, i.e., 99.99% or over.
trace: --> A.3 Impact of interference

text: A.4 Impact of dynamic capacity variations
trace: --> A.4 Impact of dynamic capacity variations

text: Microwave and mmWave Point to Point radio systems are designed to operate with high availability by allowing adequate fade margin in their link budget. The fade margin is calculated to compensate the propagation loss depending on the rain intensity in the area they intended to operate. Modern PP radio systems apply Adaptive Coding and Modulation \(ACM\) technique to boost its link capacity during the clear sky period taking advantage of the fade margin to apply higher order modulation scheme with higher capacity than the one needed during the worst raining period. This allows the PP radio system to transmit at its maximum transmission capacity allowed by the changing weather condition. This dynamic variations in the modulation method can cause deterioration to the TE, because the data size that is processed by the Modem vary significantly between the different ACM schemes. In general, in ACM technology, the packet delay varies with the modulation level. This is caused by changes in the transmission bandwidth, which results by buffer retention of packets and the mapping process to wireless frames. It is therefore necessary to ensure that equipment selected in the network for time sensitive application does not deteriorate the TE characteristics as a result of operation of the ACM technology.

text: A.5 Impact of Band and Carrier Aggregation
trace: --> A.5 Impact of Band and Carrier Aggregation

text: Wireless transport systems operate in a variety of bands ranging from the lower microwave spectrum up to the mmWave above 100 GHz. The characteristics of these bands are summarised in \[x1\], showing large bandwidth availability in mmWave spectrum but with shorter link length, while the systems operating in the lower bands of the microwave spectrum have longer links with narrower channel bandwidth is available. Band and Carrier Aggregation \(BCA\) technique combines different channels that may be even in different bands, providing a single big capacity pipe. In particular, BCA allows the combined benefits of the longer hop distance of microwave systems with the high capacity in multiple Gigabits per second of the mmWave bands such as the E-bands and above. However, this BCA pipe will have different propagations losses between the portion of the links operating in the microwave band and the one operating in the mmWave band. Furthermore, these links with multi- band operation would result in part of the links in one direction to disconnect resulting in imbalance between the go and return of the wireless transport link. As such, it is necessary to consider the effects

text: Annex B Radio operation when synchronization is lost
trace: --> Annex B Radio operation when synchronization is lost

text: This section describes the radio operational impacts during the sync loss and recommendations or best practices for Sync plane for handling the Radio operation during the sync loss. All the data processing clocks in O-RU are driven by the S-plane Reference. If S-plane is down, we might lose sync. If O-RU implements Holdover O-RU moves to Holdover state if not O-RU moves to FREE-RUN state. The M-Plane/OAM \(Operation and Maintenance modules\) detects this S-plane state changes and might initiate shutting down data processing paths and cells will be brought down to inactive state.

text: B.1 Potential impacts due to sync loss on O-RUs
trace: --> Annex B Radio operation when synchronization is lost --> B.1 Potential impacts due to sync loss on O-RUs

text: Usually O-RUs upon losing the lock \(due to PTP/Sync-E down\) might move to HOLDOVER. At this state cells are still active and continue to be operational as much as they can. The holdover duration needed to maintain the cells to be intact is subject to the holdover characteristics of the Oscillator \(ageing, holdover per day etc..\), sync accuracy. An oscillator with good holdover characteristics would lead to a slow drift such that the frequency reference is still within tolerance and the clocks don't change too much then we can continue as the cells are effectively still in sync even though they have lost the clock reference. If the frequency is out by too much then the carrier starts drifting across the spectrum - potentially starting to encroach on adjacent signals and causing signal corruption if it drifts beyond guard band. If there is a phase drift happening, then the cell timing is out, and handsets will then exhibit jumps in range that they are not expecting and handover from one cell to another may fail. Further static handsets may see ranging errors increase. During the sync loss its essential to be able to meet 50ppb frequency limit and 3us of Time error \(3GPP thresholds\) for the cells to be operational without any problems.

text: B.1.2 Impact on Handover/Handoff
trace: --> Annex B Radio operation when synchronization is lost --> B.1 Potential impacts due to sync loss on O-RUs --> B.1.2 Impact on Handover/Handoff

text: It is a very basic requirement of the system that as the mobile handset moves out of one cell to the next, it must be possible to hand the call over from the base station of the first cell, to that of the next with no discernible disruption to the call. This is termed as cell handover/handoff. It is necessary to ensure handoff can be performed reliably and without disruption to any calls. handover or handoff is one of the key performance indicators monitored so that a robust cellular handover / handoff regime is maintained on the cellular network. Sync loss on O-RU will impact the cell handoff as the RU starts drifting in phase/frequency when the handset moves from connected cell to the other and leading to call drops.

trace: --> B.2 Potential impacts due to sync loss on O-DU --> B.2.1 O-DU Sync loss in LLS-C3 topology

text: If O-DU moves to holdover due to upstream timeTransmitter sync loss, then O-DU continue to serve the connected O-RUs for the holdover duration and continues to generate the slot intervals \(TTI/SFN numbers\) towards the connected O-RUs. The L1/BBU instances on O-DU need TOD to generate SFN/slot intervals. The slot intervals are dependent on the LTE/5G TDD/FDD deployment and sub carrier spacing being used. For example, 5G Sub6 with 30KHz sub carrier spacing will need 125us for slot interval/SFN generation. Sync is needed to maintain the TOD to be able to generate these SFNs at 125us. Once the specified holdover duration expires all the carriers corresponding to this O- DU will be brought down/detached/deleted. If O-DU holdover duration is greater than O-RU in this case cells will be brought down by O-RU before the O-DU detaches the carriers. Any state changes on O-DU will be propagated as an M-Plane events \(Netconf/yang\) towards O-RU and that's how O-RU knew that O-DU is in Holdover.

* 1. In order to avoid or minimize the impact on the cell's operations, its recommended for O-RUs equipped with Oscillators having good holdover characteristics \(low drift\) for any type of sync losses.  
  * 2. For LLS-C3 deployments with multiple FH links towards O-RU, its recommended to have SyncE and PTP carried in different links so as to avoid Single point of failures for S-plane and allow to extend the O-RU holdover for longer durations with SyncE back up If link carrying PTP is down and thus minimizing the impact on cell operations, avoid cell disruptions.
  * 3. For LLS-C4 deployments where O-RU uses GNSS based local PRTC as sync source, its recommended to use GNSS Receiver with better holdover characteristics due to minimize the impact on cells during the GNSS failures. It is also a good practice to have a packet-based sync source as a backup \(G.8275.1 \[1\] full timing support or G.8275.2 \[3\] partial timing support\) so that in case of any GNSS errors, the O-RU can switchover to Packet based sync as usually the time to rectify or recover from the GNSS faults needs a site inspection which can run into multiple days and during this time the O-RU PLL might have drifted further which can affect the cells.

text: Annex C QoS Considerations for PTP packets
trace: --> Annex C QoS Considerations for PTP packets

text: To achieve high degree of accuracy of the synchronization clock recovered from PTP, important aspect of the overall solution is the precise time stamping of PTP packets.
trace: --> Annex C QoS Considerations for PTP packets

text: To achieve Class C requirements, physical layer time stamping must be implemented, since other time stamping methods, or PTP packets without timestamping at all, do not provide suitable accuracy. From the QoS perspective, PTP packets with physical layer time stamping do not require strict priority queueing to optimize packet's latency/jitter, since the queueing time is accounted by the physical layer time stamps. The only requirement is some QoS queue with guaranteed bandwidth, to avoid PTP packet drop during congestion events.
trace: --> Annex C QoS Considerations for PTP packets

text: As already discussed in sections 6.2.2 and 6.2.3 might happen, especially in mixed 3G/4G/5G deployments, that both ITU-T G.8275.1 \[1\] PTP profile \(with hop-by-hop PTPoE sessions using physical layer timestamping for PTPoE packets\) and ITU-T G.8275.2 \[3\] PTP profile \(with multi-hop PTPoIP sessions\) are used across the transport network. Depending on the transport network element capabilities, it can happen that the PTPoIP packets are not time-stamped \(i.e., T-BC/T-TC function to timestamp PTPoIP packets is missing\) on transit transport network elements. This is called PTP unaware node. In such case, PTP unaware nodes might considerably increase the latency/jitter of PTPoIP packets. Examples of possible deployments of Partial Timing Support and Assisted Partial Timing Support, with some transit routers being PTP unaware routers, are presented in Figure C-1, Figure C-2 and Figure C-3.

trace: --> Annex E Synchronization over TDM PON

text: E.1 Short introduction to TDM PON
trace: --> E.1 Short introduction to TDM PON

text: A TDM PON system is composed of an Optical Liner Termination \(OLT\) with one or more network ports and one or more PON ports, the point-to-multipoint optical distribution networks \(ODNs\) terminated by the OLT, and a set of Optical Network Units \(ONUs\) on each ODN. Each ONU then provides network connectivity to one or more "user" devices connected to it. In the case of Mobile X-haul such devices are gNBs, O-CUs, O-DUs and/or O-RUs.
trace: --> E.1 Short introduction to TDM PON

text: TDM PONs are characterized by the shared medium nature of the ODN connecting multiple ONUs to a single OLT port. The common bandwidth is shared in TDM fashion in downstream \(DS\) and TDMA fashion in upstream \(US\), with a WDM separation between downstream and upstream signals for full duplex operation. For upstream the TDMA is performed by means of a Dynamic Bandwidth Assignment \(DBA\) algorithm in the OLT that controls when each ONU can send a burst of data, so that bursts from different ONUs are interleaved at the OLT receiver without overlaps. In downstream the TDM is done by each ONU only selecting the packets that are destined to itself.
trace: --> E.1 Short introduction to TDM PON

text: Figure E-1: TDM PON system
trace: --> E.1 Short introduction to TDM PON

text: The latency for data transport is inherently asymmetrical in TDM PON;
trace: --> E.1 Short introduction to TDM PON

text:
* DS : latency by buffering in the OLT, FEC over PON, serialization of control words at line rate, fiber propagation time, queuing & scheduling in ONU
  * US: latency by TDMA in ONU \(scheduling done by DBA in OLT\), FEC over PON, serialization of control words at line rate, fiber propagation time, buffering in OLT
trace: --> E.1 Short introduction to TDM PON

text: The delay discrepancy between US and DS can be large and this means that PTP cannot be used across a TDM PON. The PON interface uses its own MAC encapsulation \(over which Ethernet-based packets are transported transparently\), meaning that plain Sync-E as such is not readily available at the ONU PON interface. Therefore, TDM PON systems have built in alternative methods for frequency and time synchronization.

text: According to \[1\], a medium-specific access section can still act as a link in the synchronization chain by means of a pair of converters between PTP and the medium, also known as Inter-Working Functions IWF. When mapping this on a TDM PON system, the ODN is the access medium, the Transport Protocol Specific Transmission Convergence \(TPS-TC\) functionality is part of the IWF in the OLT and the ONU, and the PTP timeTransmitter and timeReceiver \(in respectively ONU and OLT\) represent the other part of their IWF, see Figure E-2.

text: PTP is terminated in the OLT \(timeReceiver clock\). The time synchronization is carried over the PON medium by TPS-TC \(more details in section E3\). PTP is regenerated in each ONU \(timeTransmitter clock\) on its UNIs towards the end device \(example is an O-RU\).
The PON system functionally acts as one \(distributed\) T-BC in the sync chain. In terms of performance, it can be modelled as pair of T-BCs of the same class.

Note that this TPS-TC approach is completely independent from latency that regular traffic experiences across the PON system, so its accuracy is not linked to any QoS or traffic load dependency. The TDM PON system supports the hybrid model \(PTP + Sync-E/eSyncE\).

text: frequency synchronization
trace: --> frequency synchronization

text: In TDM PON systems there is a continuous downstream bitstream, whether it is real traffic or filling-in dummy traffic. Hence there is a continuous availability of frame structures and bit transitions.
trace: --> frequency synchronization
--> frequency synchronization

text: For ITU TDM PONs, frequency synchronization is done based on the precise framing structure \(125 µs\) of the physical medium. The OLT terminates Sync-E or eSyncE from the network, uses it for its internal clock generating the frame structure. The ONU derives its clock frequency from the 8kHz frame repetition rate and uses it to support Sync-E or eSyncE on its user interfaces. Basically, the ONU PLL is controlled by the OLT clock which is synchronized by Sync-E.

text: E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities

text: Mechanisms
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Mechanisms

text: Synchronization over TDM PON is made possible by the fact that the system is inherently synchronized between the OLT and its ONUs.
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Mechanisms

text: First, each ONU is detected and automatically "ranged", whereby the OLT measures its distance and sets time equalization per ONU, to align on it on the US TDMA scheme. For this time alignment each ONU has access to a common \(arbitrary\) time reference with the OLT \(ITU PON: D/S 125µs frame boundary\).
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Mechanisms

text: Then the correlation to ToD \(received at the OLT by PTP from the network\) is added; each ONU retrieves the absolute ToD for an association of a given event with a given timestamp. This association is communicated by the OLT to the ONU in a management message. In ITU PON the ToD \(at a hypothetical ONU, at start of PON frame X\) is communicated via OMCI to each ONU.
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Mechanisms

text: Dependencies
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Dependencies

text:
* There are several factors that impact the Time Error \(TE\) across TDM PON system \(OLT SNI ONU UNI\):
  * RTT estimation depends on speed of light, which depends on n\(λ\)
  * Variation on λ: the PON WDM bands in US and DS depend on the PON technology
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Dependencies
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Dependencies
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Dependencies
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Dependencies
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities -->

text:
* Accuracy of PON time equalization of ONUs \(correction measure to deal with ONU drifts\)
  * Knowledge of internal delays in OLT
  * Knowledge of internal delays in ONU
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities -->
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities -->

text: The Time Alignment Error \(TAE\) between two O-RU air interfaces when subtended over TDM PON depends on:
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities -->

text:
* Location of the reference clock common to both O-RUs, which depends on the topology:
  * Common PON card \(same PON port or different PON ports\): local card clock
  * Common OLT node: local OLT clock
  * Different OLTs: first common node to which both OLTs are connected
  * Accuracies of the \(relevant part of the\) TDM PON system \(the TE between the common clock reference and ONU UNI\)
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities -->
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities -->

text: Capabilities of TDM PON systems
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems

text: TDM PON standards do not provide system-wide requirements \(OLT SNI – ONU UNI\) on time synchronization performance, but it is an active area of discussion.
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems

text: The built-in mechanisms for ToD distribution across a TDM PON medium \(TPS-TC\) are very accurate, in the order of 10ns for cTE:
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems

text:
* ToD notifications in OAM messages have 1ns resolution
  * Ranging accuracy can be in the order of several ns \(below 5ns\)
  * Estimation of variations on n\(λ\) over the known WDM bands and fiber type can bring precision of factors depending on n\(λ\) down to below 5ns at 20km
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems

text: Ultimately, the full system performance \(including dTE\) is up to implementation of ONU and OLT.
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems

text: There is no standardized way yet to test/characterize TAE between multiple output ports of a system for all T-BC Class of clocks \(ITU-T standards have defined only for Class-C T-BC, but TDM PON systems do not meet this accuracy\).
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems

text: There are two ways to label a given performance of a system in function of its max|TE| between OLT SNI and ONU UNI:
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems

text:
* Either it is equivalent to a single T-BC of a given class \(refer \[2\] Table 7-1\),
  * or it is equivalent to what is expected from a pair of T-BCs of the same class \(refer \[2\] Table V.1, or formula IV-13 in \[8\] \(which has two extreme cases depending on the symmetry of |dTEL\(t\)| around cTE\)\).
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems

text: For example, for a TDM PON system that would meet max|TE| of 100ns, it would mean:
trace: -->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems
-->  --> E.3.2 TDM PON capabilities --> Capabilities of TDM PON systems

text:
* Compliance of full system to pair of Class A T-BCs \(max|TE| of 160ns as per \[2\] or 130 to 160ns as per \[8\]\)
  * Compliance of full system to pair of Class B T-BCs \(max|TE| of 100ns as per \[2\] or upper bound of 100ns as per \[8\] or single Class A T-BC \(100ns\)
  * No compliance of full system to single Class B T-BC \(interpreted as max|TE| of 70ns as per \[2\] or upper bound of 70ns as per \[8\]\)
  * No compliance of full system to pair of Class C T-BCs \(max|TE| of 45ns as per \[2\] , or upper bound of 35ns as per \[8\]\) or single Class C T-BC \(max|TE| of 30ns\)

text: Annex G Security Considerations
trace: --> Annex G Security Considerations

text: Security in Xhaul networks and specifically in Fronthaul networks for sync plane is critical for the operation of the wireless network. Encryption, Authentication and/or Architectural redundancy models are different ways to secure and mitigate the security threats of the network. This chapter describes various models that can be exercised to secure the sync plane in the Xhaul networks.
trace: --> Annex G Security Considerations

text: G.1 Architectural Redundancy Models
trace: --> G.1 Architectural Redundancy Models

text: The Authentication, Integrity protection and/or Encryption of the PTP control \(events and general\) packets do not always address the performance degradation introduced by some rogue nodes in the middle. The Architectural redundancy models in this section describes how to effectively detect and mitigate the performance degradation and other attacks.
trace: --> G.1 Architectural Redundancy Models

text: G.1.1 Network model with no sync redundancy
trace: --> G.1 Architectural Redundancy Models --> G.1.1 Network model with no sync redundancy

trace: --> G.1 Architectural Redundancy Models --> G.1.1 Network model with no sync redundancy

text:
* The topology shown in Figure G-1 does not have sync network redundancy for the transport network elements \(CSR and HSR nodes\).
  * Any attack on CSR, HSR or the points between GM to O-RU interconnects can impact the sync recovery at O-RU.
  * Sync network without redundancy is difficult to detect and mitigate the performance degradation attack.

text:
* The topology shown in Figure G-2, redundant sync paths are exercised. Every node in the chain from GM to O-RU has more than one \(two\) sync paths, green and blue color respectively.
  * Attack on any node or insertion of a rogue node in blue path can be mitigated with green path.
  * The HSR, CSR and O-RU can exercise the passive port monitoring feature described in Annex-G of ITU-T G.8275.1 profile \[1\] -" Monitoring PTP timeTransmitter port using PTP passive port" to effectively detect any change in performance between active timeReceiver port and alternate passive port.
  * Monitoring of the active timeTransmitetr using passive port does not automatically trigger the A-BTCA algorithm to switchover rather it helps to detect the time/phase change between these two ports. The network operator can monitor the changes and take necessary action as needed to mitigate the attack.
trace: --> G.1.2 Network model with sync redundancy --> Figure G-2

text: Note: With 1+1 resiliency model \(as shown in figure G-2\), it is only possible to detect the difference of the time between the passive and active PTP ports. It is not possible to predictably determine which clock/time source is correct. It is critical to have more than 2 links/PTP ports to detect the bad or rogue time source.

text: In a packet content manipulation attack, an attacker manipulates suitable fields of PTP packets in transit and affecting the clock synchronization of some or all downstream nodes. text: H.1 Introduction
trace: --> H.1 Introduction

text: The precision of a frequency/phase and time recovered at the end of the synchronization chain depends on any single node or combination of multiple nodes in the sync network. The sum of the timing errors introduced at all nodes along the synchronization path needs to be within the required timing budget for a given application. If there is an issue with nodes synchronization in a sync network chain, it is very complex to identify which node had introduced the issue.
trace: --> H.1 Introduction
--> H.1 Introduction

text: End-to-end Sync monitoring feature can be used to identify synchronization issues in the network, correlation of timing events and much more. It can be used to monitor the health of the nodes in synchronization network and assess the timing performance of the node as well as complete synchronization network chain.

--> H.1 Introduction

text: H.3.3 Dynamic Analysis
trace: -->  --> H.3.3 Dynamic Analysis

text: Dynamic analysis is a computational approach that evaluates multiple nodes or the entire synchronization network topology to facilitate error detection, correlation, and reporting. This method involves the correlation and analysis of attributes from various nodes within the synchronization chain to assess and characterize the overall behavior of the synchronization network.
trace: -->  --> H.3.3 Dynamic Analysis

text: Figure H-2: End-to-end Sync monitoring dynamic analysis model
trace: -->  --> H.3.3 Dynamic Analysis

text:
* In the event of a Radio or Application error caused by a synchronization issue, a comprehensive investigation is required to accurately identify the root cause of the problem.
  * For example, consider a scenario where both T-BC-2 and T-BC-3 are in a PTP unlocked state. While a basic static analysis model may identify that both T-BC-2 and T-BC-3 are in an unlocked state, it would fail to provide clarity on whether the O-RU is being impacted by T-BC-2, T-BC-3, or both within the synchronization chain.
  * The only way to ascertain which T-BC is impacting the O-RU's performance is by obtaining comprehensive visibility into the synchronization topology. In the absence of this information, the operator would be required to manually trace the network nodes to identify the specific node within the chain responsible for the issue.

text: Req-1: Report active sync topology:
trace: -->  --> H.3.3 Dynamic Analysis --> Req-1: Report active sync topology:

text:
* The CMS system dynamically constructs the end-to-end active PTP synchronization path from the Grandmaster \(GM\) to the end node \(timeReceiver\), including all intermediate clock nodes \(boundary clocks\) within this model.  
  * To construct the synchronization path, the CMS evaluates each node's deviceType \(T-GM, T-BC, T-TSC\) and extendedDeviceType \(O-RU-TSC, O-DU-BC\). This evaluation enables the identification of the starting point \(T-GM\) and the termination point \(T-TSC\) of the synchronization chain.
  * The CMS will then iteratively trace the parent clock of each node, starting from the timeReceiver clock and progressing upward to the T-GM, including all intermediate nodes \(T-BC\).
  * The following PTP dataset members are recommended for discovering the synchronization topology:
  * o defaultDS.clockIdentity
  * o defaultDS.ptpTelecomProfile.deviceType
  * o defaultDS.oranE2eSyncMonitoringDS.extendedDeviceType
  * o parentDS.parentPortIdentity
  * o parentDS.grandmasterIdentity
  * o portDS.state
  * o portDS.portIdentity

text: Req-2: Report PTP timing loop
trace: -->  --> H.3.3 Dynamic Analysis --> Req-2: Report PTP timing loop

text:
* A PTP timing loop arises when a circular dependency exists within the clock synchronization path of a network. Such a loop causes the clocks to continuously adjust their timing based on one another, resulting in instability and inaccurate time synchronization.
  * As illustrated in Figure H-3, consider R3 and R4 as two synchronization nodes within a ring topology. If R3 attempts to recover time from R4, while R4 simultaneously attempts to recover time from R3, a timing loop is formed. The CMS can identify this loop by examining whether the parent clock IDs reported by these two nodes reference one another.
  * The following dataset members are recommended to be monitored for detecting the timing loop:
  * o defaultDS.clockIdentity
  * o parentDS.parentPortIdentity
  * A timing loop is identified if the defaultDS.clockIdentity of R3 matches the parentDS.parentPortIdentity.clockIdentity of R4, and simultaneously, the defaultDS.clockIdentity of R4 matches the parentDS.parentPortIdentity.clockIdentity of R3.

text: H.4.2.1.1 ptpTimestampRecordDS
trace: --> 8 H.4.2 Detailed attributes/datasets --> H.4.2.1.1 ptpTimestampRecordDS

text: ptpTimestampRecordDS contains information of the raw PTP timestamps used in the node for calculating the offset from the TimeTransmitter. End-to-end sync monitoring, the raw timestamps data can provide a crucial insight into the performance and health of the synchronization network.
trace: --> 8 H.4.2 Detailed attributes/datasets --> H.4.2.1.1 ptpTimestampRecordDS
--> 8 H.4.2 Detailed attributes/datasets --> H.4.2.1.1 ptpTimestampRecordDS

text: CMS can use the four PTP timestamps t1, t2, t3 & t4 derived from the event messages to derive the Packet Delay Variation \(PDV\), upstream and downstream delays between the timeReceiver node and the timeTransmitter node in the network. CMS may use the tools to plot a graph using the timestamp information exported from the node and see how the PDV, forward and reverse delays are varying over time.
trace: --> 8 H.4.2 Detailed attributes/datasets --> H.4.2.1.1 ptpTimestampRecordDS
--> 8 H.4.2 Detailed attributes/datasets --> H.4.2.1.1 ptpTimestampRecordDS

text: For example, in a synchronization chain of nodes, if a particular node is reporting a high correction field value, it could indicate network congestion in that particular node or the node either lost the synchronization or changed its time base.

text: O-RAN.WG9.XTRP-SYN.0-R004-v07.00 This is the TimeTransmitter to TimeReceiver delay in case of Sync message and TimeReceiver to TimeTrasmitter delay in case of Del-Req message. It is calculated as : 3 \(ReceiveTimestamp – OriginTimestamp – corrField\) H.4.2.1.2: allTimeTransmitterDS allTimeTransmitterDS contains all the remote TimeTransmitter's information as seen by a node. This includes the selected timeTransmitter information as well. This dataset is primarily derived from the received announce message from various timeTransmitters. Additionally the localPriority attribute needs to be referenced from the portDS dataset using the PTP port-number. A localPriority is configured to a PTP port of the clock and it is used in A-BTCA. Each entry of the allTimeTransmitterDS contains below members: • parentDS as per IEEE 1588-2019 \[42\]. • timePropertiesDS as per IEEE1588-2019 \[42\]. • portDS.portIdentity as per IEEE 1588-2019 \[42\]. H.4.2.1.3: isSupported
trace: --> 8 H.4.2 Detailed attributes/datasets -->

text: isSupported attribute specifies whether the End-to-end sync monitoring feature is supported on a given node. It's a static boolean attribute where a True value represents the node supports End-to-end sync monitoring feature.
trace: --> 8 H.4.2 Detailed attributes/datasets -->

text: Once the connection between a sync node and CMS is authenticated, the CMS queries for this attribute and considers the node for End-to-end sync monitoring only if a value of True is received. In case of False, CMS will not process the End-to-end sync monitoring attributes from that node.
